rationale: A wins because it does the grown-up PR work: it turns missing insurer names, journal name, and methodology into gates instead of wallpaper. Its "25 Million Insured Members Can Get a Mental Health App for Free" is a real coverage/access story with a clear reporter lane. B has useful instincts, especially on methodology, but opening with "Calm goes from $70-a-year subscription" makes up a price the update never gave; that is how a pitch dies before the second sentence.
gaps_in_A: "The Wellness-to-Clinical Shift Is Arriving" overclaims from one Calm deal unless the company can supply comparable payer examples or a payer source.
"Coverage Was the Last Wall" is catchy but too absolute; access, uptake, clinical trust, and activation may still be walls.
"The prevailing belief in tech-health press is that independent university execution neutralizes industry funding" is an imported assumption, not a fact from the update.
The category and coverage angles partially overlap; they stay distinct only if one gets payer-market proof and the other gets member-access proof.
gaps_in_B: "$70-a-year subscription" is invented. The update gives 4 million paid subscribers, not price.
"consumer subscription apps survive once growth slows" invents a business condition. No slowdown is in the facts.
"how Calm gets paid when no revenue terms were disclosed" is a fair question, but it is too thin as the lead angle unless Calm can disclose payment structure on or off record.
"sponsored-research skepticism journalists are writing about right now" is a fake zeitgeist peg unless backed by current coverage. Do not smuggle trend claims into the rationale.
